one_liner: Keyed 64-bit universal string hash built on carry-less multiply; about 40% faster than CityHash64 on inputs over 64 bytes.
what_it_does: CLHash is a randomized (keyed) 64-bit hash for byte strings with a proven collision bound: XOR-universal for inputs up to 1 KB and 2.004/2^64-almost XOR-universal up to 2^64 bytes. The C API is clhash(key, buf, len) -> uint64_t, where key is a 1064-byte table you build once with get_random_key_for_clhash(seed1, seed2) and free() yourself. A C++ clhasher RAII wrapper hashes std::string, std::vector, C strings and raw object bytes. There is no streaming/incremental interface.
how_it_is_fast: The core is CLNH: each pair of 64-bit input words is XORed with key words and multiplied with a single PCLMULQDQ (PMULL on ARM), and the 128-bit products are XOR-accumulated without any reduction, because GF(2) arithmetic has no carries. Inputs over 1 KB are cut into 1 KB blocks whose CLNH results are chained by Horner's rule in GF(2^127), using a cheap 'lazy' reduction modulo 2^128+4+2 (two shifts and XORs). A final PSHUFB-table reduction modulo x^64+x^4+x^3+x+1 produces the 64-bit output. The paper puts the Haswell bound at one CLMUL per 16 bytes (0.125 cycles/byte) and measures 0.16.
when_to_use: Bulk hashing of inputs from hundreds of bytes to many KB (documents, packets, file blocks), where cycles per byte matter more than per-call latency.
Replacing CityHash64 on Haswell-or-newer x64 for inputs over 64 bytes (paper: about 40% faster there, parity at 32 bytes or less).
You need a provable collision bound from a secret random key, not just a clean SMHasher run, e.g. hash tables or sketches fed by untrusted input that cannot observe hash values.
Mixed x86-64 and AArch64 fleets that need identical hashes: the README and known-answer tests guarantee bit-for-bit equal output on both.
when_not_to_use: Short keys: rurban SMHasher measures 67.22 cycles/hash on 1-31 byte keys vs 29.46 for xxh3; issue #6 found it slower than std::hash below about 192 bytes, and lengths that are not a multiple of 8 are slower still (issue #3).

When you need every output bit to behave randomly (e.g. using low bits directly as a table index): for short inputs the default build is linear in the input. SMHasher3 fails it on 186 of 250 tests (avalanche, BIC, Sparse, Text, Seed and more), and 23 even with CLHASH_BITMIX. rurban's BITMIX log also shows mass collisions in the Sparse, Permutation, TwoBytes and PerlinNoise keysets.
Hardware without carry-less multiply: builds only on x86 with PCLMULQDQ+SSE4.2 or AArch64 with the PMULL crypto extension; POWER and other targets hit an #error.
Streaming or multi-field hashing: there is no incremental API (issue #3, open since 2016), so fields must be concatenated first.

Pure bulk speed: the xxh3 win does not replicate. SMHasher3 measures 7.36 bytes/cycle vs XXH3-64's 12.82, and on rurban's table gxhash64 (48919.73 MiB/s) and falkhash (52401.48) more than double CLHash's 22932.36.

integration.form: source-drop (one .c + one .h) or static lib (CMake, find_package(clhash))
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (C++11 for the clhasher wrapper; CMake 3.16 for the CMake build); GCC/Clang need -msse4.2 -mpclmul on x86 or -march=armv8-a+crypto on ARM; MSVC via the CMake Visual Studio generator
integration.platforms: x86-64 with PCLMULQDQ + SSE4.2 (Haswell-class or newer for full speed); AArch64 with PMULL (Apple Silicon, Graviton, modern Cortex-A); CI covers Linux x64/ARM64, macOS ARM64, Windows MSVC
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. clhash() only reads the key and input, so one shared key appears safe for concurrent calls (inferred from source).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same bytes-in, 64-bit-out shape as CityHash64WithSeed, but you must build and keep a 1064-byte key via get_random_key_for_clhash() instead of passing a 64-bit seed, and hash values differ

gotchas: Key handling: get_random_key_for_clhash() expands two seeds with xorshift128+, which is not a CSPRNG, and the source says the seeds must be non-zero. clhash() uses aligned 16-byte loads on the key, so a hand-built key must be 16-byte aligned, and the alignment check is only an assert().
The empty input hashes to 0 under every key (the known-answer vector in tests/unit.c; both the accumulator and the length term are zero).
The C++ clhasher frees its malloc'd key in its destructor but defines no copy constructor or assignment, so any copy (including copying a container that stores it) double-frees.
CLHASH_BITMIX (Murmur fmix64 finalizer) changes hash values and is applied only on the <=1024-byte path; inputs over 1 KB skip it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick CLHash over xxHash (XXH3), wyhash or rapidhash only when you want a proven universality bound from a random key, not for speed. XXH3 matches or beats it (rurban: CLHash about 10% faster in bulk; SMHasher3: XXH3-64 about 1.7x faster in bulk and 30.69 vs 48.19 cycles on 1-32 B keys), and gxhash or falkhash are over 2x faster in bulk.
verified_claims_summary: In Lemire & Kaser (J. Cryptographic Engineering 2016), built with GCC 4.8 -O2 on a 3.4 GHz i7-4770 Haswell with Turbo Boost off, the 2015 research code took 0.16 cycles/byte vs 0.23 for the authors' C port of CityHash64WithSeed 1.1.1 on 4 kB inputs, and 0.45 vs 0.48 at 64 B. SMHasher3 (hardware not stated) gives CLHash 7.36 vs CityHash-64's 4.75 bytes/cycle in bulk. rurban SMHasher (Ryzen 5 3350G, compiler not stated) gives 22932.36 vs 20853.74 MiB/s for xxh3, but 67.22 vs 29.46 cycles/hash on small keys.
